name: Crossbar Commons
award: 2025 Federal 4% and state housing tax credits (Round Two)
headline: Mercy Housing Mountain Plains plans Crossbar Commons, a new four-story building with 104 family apartments for households earning 30% to 50% AMI, on city-owned land at 15961 E. Colfax Ave. in north Aurora. It won 2025 Round Two federal 4%, state and TOC credits from CHFA.
why_it_matters: It is the first project from Aurora's land-banking program: the city bought the site in 2022, leases it for $100 a year and adds a $2.5M soft loan, which lets the deal reach 50% AMI and below without project-based vouchers.

status.label: Credits awarded; bond hearing held July 2026; closing not confirmed
status.detail: The Aurora Housing Authority set a bond (TEFRA) hearing for 2026-07-29 on up to $14,000,000 of bonds for the project. The application targeted a financial closing in September 2026, but no public record of a closing, building permit or groundbreaking was found.

next_step: Watch for the Aurora mayor's bond approval, the bond closing and a building permit or groundbreaking notice, and for the city's ground lease and loan documents.

key_numbers.meaning: 51 one-bedroom, 35 two-bedroom, 15 three-bedroom and 3 four-bedroom units: 6 at 30% AMI and 98 at 50% AMI.
About $20.7M over 10 years, plus $1,800,000 in state credit and $135,200 in TOC credit.
CHFA lists itself as issuer. The Aurora Housing Authority later noticed a hearing on up to $14M of its own bonds for the project.

key_numbers.value: City land plus a $2.5M soft loan
key_numbers.meaning: A long-term ground lease at $100 a year on land the applicant values at $1.6M, and a subordinate low-interest cash-flow loan, per the application.

background.text: The City of Aurora bought the 15961 E. Colfax Ave. and 15978 E. 16th Ave. parcels in 2022 and in July 2023 issued its first housing development RFP for them, asking for a multifamily project with over 75% affordable units and offering the winner a License and Option to Lease Agreement.
The city picked Mercy Housing through that competitive process in 2023. The application calls the project the first initiative of the city's new land-banking program for affordable housing.

The project was first called something else; the application attaches a narrative on the name change. The owner entity named in the bond notice is MHMP 22 Aurora Global LLLP. The name Crossbar refers to nearby soccer facilities.

Mercy dropped the higher-AMI units from its first unit mix after partner feedback, so that every unit serves households at or below 50% AMI. It held two public workshops (MLK Library and Soccer City) and reports no opposition.
The market study reports a 15.0% overall capture rate and 2.1% vacancy for 30% and 50% AMI units in the market area, against 6.9% overall, and expects lease-up at 20 units a month.
The applicant says the only other family properties in the market area with all units at 50% AMI or below rely on project-based vouchers. Crossbar Commons has no project-based vouchers.

At application, Mercy had finished concept review with the city and planned to complete site plan approval and get a building permit in time to close in September 2026, using Aurora's expedited permit review for affordable housing.

A full-time resident services coordinator will run Mercy's family services model. Residents also get free Esusu rent reporting, Soccer City memberships and RTD NECO passes, which are paid from the operating budget.

discrepancies.text: CHFA's award report and the application name CHFA as bond issuer, while the Aurora Housing Authority's July 2026 hearing notice has the Housing Authority issuing up to $14,000,000 of bonds for the project.
The application planned $21,900,000 of tax-exempt construction bonds, while CHFA's award report lists $13,940,000 of bonds and the Housing Authority notice caps the bonds at $14,000,000.

open_questions: Aurora City Council or staff approvals of the ground lease and the $2.5M city loan (dates, resolution numbers, final terms) were not found in public records.
Which agency finally issues the bonds, whose volume cap is used, and whether the Aurora mayor approved the bonds after the July 2026 hearing.
Whether the financing closed in September 2026 as planned, and building permit and groundbreaking dates.
Total development cost, equity investor and price, first-mortgage lender, and the Mercy Community Capital loan amount.
Ground lease length, the CHFA LURA affordability period and the terms of the Aurora Housing Authority tax-exemption partnership.
